```{python}
import polars as pl 
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *
import polars.selectors as cs
# add the additional libraries you need to import for ML here

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

data_url = "https://byuidatascience.github.io/DS250-Course-Polars/Data/StarWars_with_emails.csv"
```

<!-- The first 10 rows are not part of the datset we need.

The columns headers are split across two rows. We need to clean and simplify the column headers-->

```{python}
# Read in and tidy up the first row
a = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows = 10, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding = 'utf8-lossy').row(0))
# Note the non-aschii character in the column "Do you consider yourself to be a fan of the Expanded Universe". (column AF if you open it in Excel). 

# BTW: Detecting what it is and where can be difficult

# Lossy means that invalid utf8 values are replaced with � characters. When using other encodings than utf8 or utf8-lossy, the input is first decoded in memory with python. Defaults to utf8...ignore_errors = True does not replace the non-utf8 character with a blank space like you would hope

a[2] = "seen_any" #simply overwrite the value at index 2

# Rather than changing each column header manually,
# here we use regex to apply changes more efficiently
a = (
  a.str.replace(r".+seen.+", "seen_")
   .str.replace(r".+rank.+", "rank_")
   .str.replace(r"(.+favorably.+)", "fav_")
   .fill_null(strategy = "forward")

   .str.replace("\uFFFD+", "") #this gets rid of the question marks in a diamond characters 
   .str.strip_chars()
   .str.to_lowercase()
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .str.replace(r"location(.+)", "location")

)
a[3] = "star_wars_fan"
a[30] = "who_shot_first"
a[31] = "know_expanded_universe"
a[32] = "expanded_universe_fan"
a[33] = "star_trek_fan"
```

<!-- Combine series q and a into one series to be used as column names-->

```{python}
b = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows = 11, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding = 'utf8-lossy').row(0))

b = (
  b.str.replace(r"Star Wars: (Episode \w+) .+", "${1}")
   .str.replace("Response", "")
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .fill_null("")
   .str.strip_chars()
)

```

```{python}
#Now combine the two series, each of which contains part of the desired column header
new_names = (a + b).to_list()

# Read in the data, skipping over the column header rows
# and use 'new_names' as the column headers
df = pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows=12, has_header=False, new_columns = new_names )
```

## Executive Summary

- **Problem:** the client wants respondent contact info parsed out of the survey export, the dataset validated against the original FiveThirtyEight article, and a model that predicts whether a respondent earns $50k+, to support a marketing and ML initiative.
- **Data:** FiveThirtyEight's 2014 "Star Wars" survey (1,000+ respondents), with fictitious emails added for this project.
- **Findings so far:** every respondent's email was split into first name, last name, and domain using domain-specific regex; domain casing was standardized so usage counts aren't fragmented by case.
- **Stretch goal:** not attempted in this submission.
- **Still pending:** the two article-validation charts and the $50k classification model (see Methods/Results).

## Methods

Before anything else, `df`'s column headers had to be rebuilt — the CSV stores them across two separate rows underneath 10 rows of metadata (setup code above), and regex standardizes the labels and drops a stray encoding artifact in the Expanded Universe fan column so the rest of the analysis has clean names to work with.

The `email` column also doubles as a source of respondent names. Emails follow three formats depending on domain: `first.last@gmail` (dot-separated), `last_first@yahoo` (underscore-separated), and `lastDIGITSfirst@myorg` (no separator, digits between names). A single regex pattern can't cover all three, so `pl.when/then` branches the extraction based on which separator is present.

```{python}
# Clean up stray whitespace in emails first
df = df.with_columns(pl.col("email").str.strip_chars().alias("email"))

# Extract first name, last name, and domain (regex varies by email format)
df = df.with_columns([
    pl.col("email").str.extract(r"@(.+)$", 1).str.to_lowercase().alias("email_domain"),
    pl.when(pl.col("email").str.contains(r"\."))
      .then(pl.col("email").str.extract(r"^([a-zA-Z]+)\.", 1))
      .when(pl.col("email").str.contains(r"_"))
      .then(pl.col("email").str.extract(r"_([a-zA-Z]+)@", 1))
      .otherwise(pl.col("email").str.extract(r"^([a-zA-Z]+)\d+", 1))
      .alias("first_name"),
    pl.when(pl.col("email").str.contains(r"\."))
      .then(pl.col("email").str.extract(r"\.([a-zA-Z]+)@", 1))
      .when(pl.col("email").str.contains(r"_"))
      .then(pl.col("email").str.extract(r"^([a-zA-Z]+)_", 1))
      .otherwise(pl.col("email").str.extract(r"^([a-zA-Z]+)\d+([a-zA-Z]+)@", 2))
      .alias("last_name"),
])

df.select(["email", "first_name", "last_name", "email_domain"]).head(5)
```

Every row falls into exactly one of the three branches, so each respondent ends up with a `first_name` and `last_name` pulled straight from their email string. Worth a quick visual scan of the rendered table for stray nulls, which would flag a fourth email format the regex doesn't cover yet.

`email_domain` is the one categorical variable touched so far, and it needed cleaning before it's usable: casing was inconsistent (`GMAIL`, `gmail`, `GmaiL`), which would otherwise split the same provider into multiple rows in a count table. Lowercasing it first keeps the counts accurate.

```{python}
# Domain counts (lowercased already, so case variants collapse together)
domain_counts = (
    df.group_by("email_domain")
    .agg(pl.len().alias("count"))
    .sort("count", descending=True)
)
domain_counts
```

Respondents cluster into three providers — Gmail, Yahoo, and the client's internal `myorg` domain — matching the three email formats used to build the regex above.
